title: Bournemouth closing in on appointing Marco Rose as Andoni Iraola replacement
content:
Bournemouth are in advanced negotiations to appoint Marco Rose as their new head coach to succeed Andoni Iraola, who will leave at the end of the season.

Rose, who previously coached Bundesliga sides Borussia Dortmund and RB Leipzig, has been out of work since being sacked by Leipzig in March 2025.

No agreement has yet been finalised and no announcement is expected this week, but terms are not expected to be an issue.

The 49-year-old began his coaching career with German fourth-tier club Lokomotive Leipzig in 2012 but was dismissed the following year and subsequently joined Red Bull Salzburg’s academy setup.

He was named head coach in 2017 and won the Austrian Bundesliga in his two seasons at the club, before leaving to join Borussia Monchengladbach for the 2019-20 campaign. He was there for two years before moving to Dortmund, where he spent just one season. He was hired by Leipzig in September 2022 and won the DFB-Pokal with the side in 2o23.

Bournemouth confirmed on April 14 that Iraola would leave the club at the end of the campaign, following the expiration of his contract. The Spaniard described as “right moment to step away” after three seasons at the club. Under Iraola, Bournemouth finished 12th in 2023-24, ninth in 2024-25 and are currently 11th in the Premier League table – but just three points from sixth and unbeaten in 12 matches.

Iraola also oversaw the development of players such as Milos Kerkez, Dean Huijsen and Antoine Semenyo, who went on to secure high-profile moves to Liverpool, Real Madrid and Manchester City, respectively.

Analysis by football data writer Thom Harris

Marco Rose has been out of a job since he was dismissed by RB Leipzig in March 2025, but was a leading proponent of the high-pressing football at the Red Bull multi-club network, currently overseen by former Liverpool coach Jurgen Klopp.

Gegenpressing is at the heart of the group’s tactical model — looking to win the ball back quickly after losing it, something that clearly appeals to Bournemouth.

At their best, Rose’s Leipzig side were an intimidating force, going 16 unbeaten, winning the German Cup and averaging over 2.0 goals per game throughout his first season in charge. He got the best out of attacking talents Xavi Simons, Benjamin Sesko and Lois Openda; no Bundesliga side took more shots (90) or scored more goals (23) via fast breaks while the Austrian was in charge.

Volatility is inherent in the Red Bull model, built upon a rotating cast of young players with high potential who can take time to settle or suffer from losses of form. Rose struggled to turn the tide when results faltered in winter 2024, finding it hard to impose his all-or-nothing style on a weakened squad lacking in athleticism and confidence in midfield.

That said, Rose’s pedigree has rightly attracted Bournemouth, a manager with 45 games under his belt in the Champions League, a double title-winner in Austria, and with four top-four finishes in the German top-flight to his name across three different clubs.

His commitment to a courageous style of play — vertical, aggressive and fast — clearly gels with a team who have consistently punched above their weight, approaching their football in much the same way.
